chunks.content: Junior School Agriculture is a five-year course (Grade 3 to 7) designed to promote learners' psychomotor skills, cognitive ability and practical techniques. It is a science learning area involving both theory and practical activities, giving learners opportunities to identify, investigate, solve problems, carry out agricultural activities, and assess their viability sustainably. Since Zimbabwe's economy is agro-based, the syllabus aims to help learners acquire agricultural knowledge, skills and positive attitudes at grassroots level so they can be proactive in their community and the national economy, value the dignity of labour, and harness enterprise opportunities. The syllabus also serves as a foundation for Secondary School Agriculture.

The Junior Agriculture syllabus covers 8 topics, taught across all grades with increasing breadth and depth: (1) Introduction to Agriculture, (2) Climate and Land Use, (3) Soil, (4) Water, (5) Plants, (6) Animals, (7) Farm Implements and Machinery, and (8) Agribusiness. This syllabus covers theory and practical activities in water, soil, plant and animal management, farm tools and machinery, and agri-business, seeking to develop skills in sustainable soil and water management, production and maintenance of agricultural produce, and marketing/value addition.

The Agriculture syllabus develops learners' appreciation of gender equity, Heritage Studies and teamwork, and equips them to deal with disaster risk management, food security, and safety and health issues. Learners should be able to integrate indigenous knowledge systems with new technology to address emerging environmental challenges. The syllabus assumes learners already know: various plants and animals; how to conduct practical activities such as weeding, digging and watering; how to use basic tools such as hoes, slashers and wheelbarrows; that buying and selling of agricultural produce takes place; and that resources such as land, tools and equipment are available for use.

chunks.topic: Importance of Agriculture and Farm Tool Classification (Grade 3)
chunks.content: Learners explain the importance of agriculture to the community and the nation, and learn to use farm tools safely. Content covers the importance of agriculture to the community and nation, and classification of farm tools by use: digging tools, cutting tools, watering tools, and spraying tools, along with the safe use of farm tools and implements.
learning_activities: Educational touring to observe commercial agricultural activities
Matching tools to their uses and collecting/grouping tools according to use
Sketching farm tools and designing/keeping an inventory of farm tools
Discussing and demonstrating the safe use of farm tools and implements

chunks.content: Learners identify the seasons of Zimbabwe and identify signs from their local environment that indicate season changes. Content covers Zimbabwe's four agricultural seasons: the rain season, post-rain season, cool dry season, and hot dry season.
learning_activities: Naming the seasons and classifying which months fall within each season
Discussing local activities and events done in each season
Listing environmental signs (including indigenous knowledge systems) that indicate seasonal changes
Singing songs, reciting rhymes and poems related to the seasons

chunks.topic: Soil, Compost Making and Soil Erosion (Grade 3)
chunks.content: Learners define soil and identify local soils, identify materials used for making compost, and define soil erosion and identify signs of it in the local environment. Content covers the importance of soil, local soils, compost making, and soil erosion with its warning signs.
learning_activities: Discussing soil and its importance; collecting samples of local soils
Collecting compost materials, pegging a compost site, making a compost heap and maintaining it
Educational tour to identify signs of soil erosion in the local environment

chunks.content: Learners state the uses of water in agriculture, covering irrigation, cleaning garden tools, and watering animals. The Grade 3 assessment focus is on correct uses of water without wastage, such as irrigating crops and cleaning garden tools responsibly.
learning_activities: Demonstrating uses of water in agriculture such as irrigating, cleaning garden tools and watering animals

chunks.topic: Local Plants, Nutrients, Vegetables, Crops and Ornamentals (Grade 3)
chunks.content: Learners identify plants within the local environment, state local organic sources of plant nutrients, identify local vegetables and classify them as indigenous or exotic, identify local field crops and fruit trees, and define/identify ornamental plants, plus define forestry and the uses of trees. Content covers plants in the local environment, local organic nutrient sources, indigenous versus exotic vegetables, local field crops and fruit trees, ornamental horticulture, and uses of trees.
learning_activities: Naming plants and collecting plant samples; educational tour to identify plants
Stating locally available organic nutrient sources for plants
Identifying local field crops, and listing/identifying local fruit trees
Describing ornamental horticulture and identifying ornamental plants

chunks.topic: Domestic Animals, Feeds, Small Livestock and Apiculture (Grade 3)
chunks.content: Learners list uses of domestic animals, identify types of animal feeds and classify them as natural or commercial, name types of small livestock (poultry or rabbits), define apiculture (beekeeping), and distinguish bees from other insects. Content covers uses of domestic animals, animal feeds, types of small livestock, and apiculture/characteristics of bees.
learning_activities: Naming domestic animals and discussing their uses; drawing and modelling domestic animals
Grouping animal feeds as natural or commercial feeds; feeding animals kept at the school
Drawing and educational touring to observe types of poultry or rabbits
Describing the differences between bees and other insects; drawing the bee

chunks.content: Learners identify types of farm implements. Assessment focuses on correct identification and drawing of farm implements, building the foundation for more advanced farm machinery study in later grades.
learning_activities: Identifying and drawing farm implements
Educational touring to observe farm implements
Keeping an inventory of farm implements

chunks.content: Learners list local agricultural products, building an early foundation for the agribusiness/enterprise strand that develops further in later grades (marketing, value addition, and running agriculture as an enterprise are introduced progressively as learners move through Grade 3-7).
learning_activities: Naming and collecting agricultural products
Drawing agricultural products

chunks.content: The overall aims that guide teaching across all Junior Agriculture grades are: to help learners appreciate the importance of agriculture to the individual, family and country; develop a positive attitude towards agriculture and its study as a science; develop environmental awareness and actively participate in conservation projects within the school and community; develop agricultural business skills in running agriculture as an enterprise; and contribute to the improvement of community nutritional needs, food security and the socio-economic development of the country.

chunks.topic: How to Make Compost - Step by Step
chunks.content: Compost is decomposed organic matter used to improve soil fertility. To make a compost heap: (1) Choose a shaded, well-drained site near the garden. (2) Dig a shallow pit or mark out an area roughly 1-2m wide. (3) Layer materials: start with coarse material (dry stalks, twigs) at the base for drainage and airflow, then alternate layers of 'green' nitrogen-rich material (fresh grass cuttings, vegetable peels, manure) with 'brown' carbon-rich material (dry leaves, straw, dry grass). (4) Add a layer of soil or manure every 2-3 layers to introduce decomposing organisms. (5) Water each layer lightly to keep the heap moist but not waterlogged. (6) Turn the heap every 2-3 weeks with a fork to add oxygen, which speeds up decomposition and prevents bad odours. (7) Compost is ready in roughly 6-10 weeks when it turns dark brown, crumbly, and earthy-smelling with no recognisable original materials. Good compost improves soil structure, water retention, and nutrient content, and is a key sustainable alternative or supplement to chemical fertiliser.

chunks.topic: Causes, Signs and Prevention of Soil Erosion
chunks.content: Soil erosion is the wearing away and loss of the fertile top layer of soil, mainly caused by water (rain runoff, especially on slopes with no vegetation cover) and wind (particularly on dry, exposed, bare soil). Signs of soil erosion include: gullies (deep channels cut into the land by running water), rills (small, shallow channels), exposed plant roots, sediment deposits after rain, and bare patches where topsoil has washed or blown away. Prevention and control methods include: contour ploughing (ploughing along the natural contours of a slope rather than up and down it, which slows water flow), building contour ridges/bunds to trap runoff water, maintaining vegetation cover (avoiding overgrazing and deforestation), mulching (covering bare soil with plant material to protect it from rain impact and wind), planting cover crops, and constructing terraces on steep slopes. Soil erosion reduces agricultural productivity because it strips away the nutrient-rich topsoil that crops depend on.

chunks.topic: Indigenous vs Exotic Vegetables - Examples and Differences
chunks.content: Indigenous vegetables are those native to Zimbabwe/Southern Africa and traditionally grown by local communities before wide introduction of foreign crops. Common examples include: muboora/nyeve (pumpkin leaves), tsunga/rugare (a type of rape/mustard-like leafy green), nyevhe (a wild spinach-type leaf), mowa (blackjack leaves), and derere (okra/jute mallow leaves, valued for their mucilaginous, slimy texture used in relishes). Exotic vegetables were introduced from elsewhere and include: cabbage, carrots, tomatoes, onions, and modern rape varieties (covo). Indigenous vegetables are generally more drought-tolerant, adapted to local soils and climate, and rich in vitamins and minerals, making them an important, resilient food security resource, especially in dry seasons or on poorer soils where exotic vegetables may struggle.

Plants need nutrients to grow, and local organic (natural, non-chemical) sources of these nutrients include: kraal/animal manure (from cattle, goats, chickens - rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium), compost (decomposed plant and kitchen waste), green manure (crops like legumes ploughed back into the soil while still green, which release nutrients as they decompose and, in the case of legumes, also fix nitrogen from the air into the soil via root nodules), ash from burnt wood or crop residues (a source of potassium), and leaf litter/mulch that decomposes naturally. Using organic nutrient sources builds long-term soil health and structure, unlike chemical fertilisers which can degrade soil biology over time if used without organic matter alongside them.

chunks.topic: Classifying Animal Feeds - Natural vs Commercial
chunks.content: Animal feeds are classified as natural (found or grown locally without industrial processing, e.g. grass, hay, crop residues like maize stover, kitchen scraps, natural browse/leaves) or commercial (manufactured/purchased feeds, formulated and often fortified, e.g. dairy meal, layers' mash, broiler starter/grower/finisher feed, pig concentrate). Commercial feeds are typically formulated to precise nutritional standards for a specific animal type and production stage (e.g. layers' mash is formulated for egg-laying hens, with added calcium for eggshell formation), while natural feeds vary in nutrient content depending on season, pasture quality and preparation. Good livestock management often combines both: natural grazing/browse as a base, supplemented with commercial feed for animals in higher-demand production stages (lactating, laying, growing).

Apiculture is the practice of keeping bees, primarily for honey and beeswax production, and also for pollination benefits to crops. Bees are distinguished from other insects by features including: their characteristic body shape (head, thorax, abdomen with a narrow 'waist'), branched/feathery body hairs that trap pollen, two pairs of wings, and their social organisation into colonies with a queen (the only breeding female, who lays all the eggs), worker bees (non-reproductive females who forage, build comb and defend the hive), and drones (males, whose main role is mating with a queen). Beehives can be traditional (e.g. hollow log hives) or modern (e.g. Langstroth or top-bar hives, which allow easier honey harvesting without destroying the comb). Beekeeping is valued in Agribusiness as a relatively low-input enterprise that also boosts crop pollination and yields on the surrounding farm.

chunks.topic: Common Farm Implements and Their Uses
chunks.content: Common hand tools/implements and their uses: hoe (digging, weeding, ridging soil), rake (levelling soil, gathering leaves/debris), spade/shovel (digging, moving loose soil or compost), fork/garden fork (turning compost, loosening soil, harvesting root crops), slasher (cutting grass and weeds), watering can (hand-watering plants), wheelbarrow (transporting soil, compost, produce or tools around the farm), axe (cutting/chopping wood), and sprayer (applying pesticides, herbicides or foliar fertiliser as a fine mist). Larger machinery introduced in later grades includes the plough (for turning and preparing soil ahead of planting, drawn by animals or a tractor) and the tractor itself, which powers various attached implements for ploughing, harrowing, planting and harvesting on a larger scale than hand tools allow.

Agribusiness treats farming as an enterprise, not just subsistence production. Value addition means processing a raw agricultural product into a more refined, higher-value product before selling it - for example, turning raw maize into mealie-meal, milk into yoghurt or cheese, or fresh tomatoes into dried tomatoes or sauce. Value addition increases income because processed products typically sell for more than raw produce and can be stored/transported more easily. Basic marketing concepts covered include: identifying a target market (who will buy the product), pricing (covering production costs plus a profit margin), and understanding supply and demand (when a product is scarce, prices tend to rise; when it is abundant, prices tend to fall). Agribusiness also connects to broader Financial Mathematics concepts such as calculating profit, loss, and cost of production.

Irrigation is the artificial application of water to crops to supplement or replace rainfall. Common methods include: furrow irrigation (water is channelled along shallow trenches between crop rows, allowing it to soak into the root zone - simple and low-cost but can waste water through evaporation and runoff), overhead/sprinkler irrigation (water is sprayed over crops from above, mimicking rainfall, giving more even coverage), drip irrigation (water is delivered slowly and directly to the base of each plant through small tubes/emitters - the most water-efficient method, minimising evaporation and runoff, though it has a higher initial setup cost), and watering cans/hand watering (practical for small gardens or seedlings). Choice of irrigation method depends on water availability, crop type, farm size, and budget - drip irrigation is especially valuable in drought-prone areas because it conserves water while still meeting crop needs.

Domestic animals serve multiple purposes on a Zimbabwean farm/homestead: cattle provide draught power (pulling ploughs and carts), milk, meat, manure for fertiliser, and hides; they are also a store of wealth and used in cultural/ceremonial contexts such as lobola (bride price). Goats and sheep provide meat, milk (goats) and manure, and are often more resilient to drought than cattle. Poultry (chickens) provide eggs and meat and require relatively low investment. Pigs provide meat and manure. Donkeys provide draught power for pulling carts and ploughs, especially valued for their hardiness. Rabbits provide meat and are a low-space, fast-breeding livestock option suitable for smaller homesteads or schools.
